posts.note: 2025-01-05 repost of a ~Feb 2022 article on Abbott's Texas order with a new intro ('a time capsule'). Most calls sit in the 2022 body and concern med-mal and ERISA consequences; flagged as time-capsule claims. One dated call ('returns in 2023') had passed by the repost date.
RAMHT SF 2025 event promo introducing Eric Vanderhoef and Chris Aiken. Calls are event lineup/attendance (own event) plus two general claims about rapid-acting treatments.
Productivity essay crediting Siri, Grammarly and MDHub.ai. Only event-lineup calls for RAMHT SF 2025 (Jan 12) logged.
Grief essay after a friend's loss. Generic grief predictions ('There will be anger') treated as truisms and not logged; one present-tense trend claim about suicide deaths logged for recall.

Satire about an Israeli agtech company also named Fermata raising $10M. Joke claims made inside the pretend-it-was-us frame (funding-round problems, locust plagues) do not read as sincere and were not logged; 'Most startup founders are not going to succeed' treated as a truism.
Music essay about the band American Football; only a next-day writing plan logged.
Meditation on the January 2025 LA fires; one vague general claim about humans continuing to tame natural forces logged for recall.
Prior-authorization essay with a 'tell me to my face' proposal. Logged the prediction that insurers will not give up prior auth without a fight and the conditional effect of the proposal.
Walkthrough of the JAMA Netw Open psilocybin RCT in pandemic healthcare workers (Back et al. 2024). Trial analysis is retrospective; one general recruitment claim and one own-event line logged.

statements.quote: on the eve of new administration that's even more anti-trans than Texas alone
statements.context: New January 2025 introduction to the reposted 2022 Texas article. The author asserts that the incoming US administration will be even more anti-trans than Texas has been.
statements.horizon_text: on the eve of new administration
statements.note: Characterization of an incoming administration's expected policy stance; borderline forecast.

statements.quote: to do otherwise is a catastrophe when it comes to civil litigation
statements.context: 2025 intro restating the article's thesis: withholding compassionate care for gender non-conforming youth (as Texas did) produces a civil-litigation catastrophe (med-mal and ERISA suits) for the state's providers and plans.
statements.note: 2025 restatement of the 2022 article's central call ('The point remain the same').

statements.quote: It's a contravention of the standards of professional ethics for doctors, so should not be a needle in a haystack to find those with legal standing.
statements.context: 2022 body. The author urges the ACLU to arrange a med-mal suit against a physician found liable after complying with Abbott's child-abuse reporting mandate, and expects plaintiffs with standing to be easy to find.
statements.confidence_phrase: should not be a needle in a haystack
statements.note: Time-capsule claim from the 2022 body; attached to advice to the ACLU. 'should' here is predictive (ease of finding plaintiffs), not normative.

statements.quote: If I can't provide the standard of care and Something Happens to a kid because I was legally prevented to do so, I don't see how I would win in that case.
statements.context: Quoted private message from a child psychiatry colleague in Florida who called two malpractice carriers (American Professional Agency, Allied World) about anticipated legislation barring standard-of-care treatment; the colleague expects to lose a med-mal case if barred from providing care. The author says his own carrier gave 'predictably the same answer'.
statements.confidence_phrase: I don't see how I would win
statements.note: Third-party quote; the author corroborates it and restates the call as his own later ('If sued, she can and should lose'). 2022 body.

statements.quote: It also opens the clinic up to almost unfathomable medico-legal liability.
statements.context: 2022 body. Texas Children's Hospital (Baylor College of Medicine) paused its Gender Affirming Medicine program after Abbott's order; the author claims the pause exposes the clinic to enormous medico-legal liability.
statements.note: Time-capsule claim from the 2022 body.

statements.quote: the imminent collapse of the very Texas Department of Family Protective Services
statements.context: 2022 body. The author predicts the Texas DFPS will collapse because Abbott's mandate makes the agency's own failure to investigate reportable to itself.
entities: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services
statements.note: Time-capsule claim from the 2022 body.

statements.quote: This could lead to a möbius loop of iterative reports of failures to protect kids.
statements.context: 2022 body. Same DFPS self-reporting paradox: hedged prediction of recursive failure-to-protect reports inside the agency.
entities: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services
statements.note: Time-capsule claim from the 2022 body.

statements.quote: Political Action as new agency mission— over the objections of civil servants— is a poor employee retention plan in Child Protection circles, I would imagine.
statements.context: 2022 body. The author expects DFPS staff attrition because the anti-trans directive conflicts with the child-protection mission employees signed up for.
entities: Texas Department of Family and Protective Services
statements.note: Time-capsule claim from the 2022 body.

statements.quote: If sued, she can and should lose. Subsequently her insurance would have to pay out on the claim.
statements.context: 2022 body. Hypothetical Texas telehealth child psychiatrist on an ER shift who must report a gender-dysphoric suicidal child's parents under Abbott's mandate; the author predicts she would lose a malpractice suit and her insurer would pay out.
statements.note: Compound conditional inside a hypothetical scenario; 'should' is predictive here. Time-capsule claim from the 2022 body.

statements.quote: Federal oversight of adequacy returns in 2023.
statements.context: 2022 body, ERISA/ACA network-adequacy section. Dated claim that federal oversight of health-plan network adequacy (time/distance, provider counts, wait times) returns in 2023.
statements.note: Written in the 2022 body; 2023 had passed by the 2025-01-05 repost date, so forward_looking is false relative to the post date.

statements.quote: They make the standard of care illegal, and pretty quickly, the sequela of that — medical malpractice lawsuits, doctors fleeing your state, etc— create what some of us in healthcare advocacy would consider an opportunity
statements.context: 2022 body. Predicted consequences of Abbott's order: medical malpractice lawsuits and doctors leaving Texas 'pretty quickly', which in turn create ERISA plan insufficiencies.
statements.note: Compound claim (lawsuits + physician flight). Time-capsule claim from the 2022 body.

statements.quote: They create ERISA plan insufficiencies that are clear and unambiguous. This opens the door for definitive enforcement of the fiduciary rule under the CA 2020 law.
statements.context: 2022 body. The author predicts that Texas anti-trans policy makes ERISA network-adequacy violations easy to prove and enables enforcement of the broker/plan-sponsor fiduciary rule from the Consolidated Appropriations Act.
statements.confidence_phrase: opens the door for definitive enforcement
statements.note: Time-capsule claim from the 2022 body.

statements.quote: how unbelievably easy it would be to make a claim against a Texas employer purchasing a theoretically ERISA compliant plan in the state of Texas
statements.context: 2022 body. The author claims ERISA fiduciary claims against Texas employers and their health plans would be very easy, citing infinite wait time, out-of-state travel distance and zero in-state providers for youth gender-affirming care.
statements.note: Time-capsule claim from the 2022 body.

statements.quote: All of them will go to jail if they do so.
statements.context: 2022 body, Q&A illustration of ERISA insufficiency: the number of providers of gender-affirming care for trans youth in Texas is zero because any who provide it 'will go to jail' under Abbott's order.
statements.note: Hyperbolic legal-consequence claim inside a rhetorical illustration; logged for recall. Time-capsule claim from the 2022 body.

statements.quote: causes every Texas employer – plan sponsors, most — and every Texas insurance plan selling ERISA compliant insurance A Serious Problem
statements.context: 2022 body. Claim that removing the gender-medicine subspecialty and its providers from Texas puts every Texas ERISA plan sponsor and insurer in legal jeopardy under federal network-adequacy and fiduciary rules.
statements.note: Time-capsule claim from the 2022 body.

statements.quote: I've been waiting for the ability to have a ERISA attorney file lawsuits that are just going to totally crush noncompliant plans.
statements.context: 2022 body, closing section. The author expects ERISA fiduciary lawsuits, enabled by Texas policy, to crush noncompliant health plans.
statements.note: Time-capsule claim from the 2022 body; author is a would-be litigant/advocate.

statements.quote: More hope is coming, too.
statements.context: RAMHT SF 2025 event promo. After saying clinicians need to know there is hope now for their patients, the author asserts more rapid-acting mental health treatments are coming.
statements.note: Vague, undated call about the rapid-acting treatment pipeline.

statements.quote: Payers need to know that these treatments can change the landscape of reimbursement and risk management.
statements.context: RAMHT SF 2025 event promo. Claim that rapid-acting mental health treatments can change payer reimbursement and risk management.
statements.note: Borderline: 'need to know' is normative framing but the embedded claim is a capability/expectation about payers; logged for recall.

statements.quote: These discussions will join Grady Hannah , Carlene MacMillan, MDhub.ai , Sanmai , Videra Health , GrayMatters Health , Fermata , Acacia Clinics , Nightware , and others that we hash out what the rapid activity future looks like.
statements.context: Lineup for RAMHT SF 2025 (January 12, 2025): discussions with Eric Vanderhoef and Chris Aiken will join the listed participants, including the author's own organizations (Fermata, Acacia Clinics, Videra Health).
statements.note: Own-event lineup claim (RAMHT, Fermata, Acacia, Videra); CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: If we are lucky, the team from Radial might be skulking around, and I have it on good authority other movers and shakers like Fred Ma and Anthony Sterns from iRxReminder will be hanging out.
statements.context: RAMHT SF 2025 attendance: Radial (author's organization) may attend; Fred Ma and Anthony Sterns of iRxReminder will attend.
statements.note: Compound: hedged (Radial) plus firm (iRxReminder) attendance claims for the author's own event; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: We are bringing live demos of things— here and now—the future of rapid-acting mental health diagnostics and treatments.
statements.context: RAMHT SF 2025 promo inside a productivity essay: this year's event will feature live demos of rapid-acting mental health diagnostics and treatments.
statements.note: Own-event programming claim; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: MDHub.ai will be at RAMHT SF 2025. Join us this Sunday, the 12th!
statements.context: MDHub.ai, the AI medical-note tool the author credits for his output, will attend RAMHT SF 2025 on Sunday, January 12, 2025.
statements.note: Own-event attendance claim; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: That having been said, death by suicide is going up.
statements.context: Grief essay after a friend's loss to suicide or overdose. The author states that deaths by suicide are rising, then cites a Rochester Epidemiology Project cohort on completed suicide after attempts.
statements.note: Present-tense trend claim about US suicide deaths, not an explicit future call; logged for recall with forward_looking false.

statements.quote: I'm a little upset that they stepped on my corporate brand, and there may be some subsequent trademark issues
statements.context: An Israeli agtech company also named Fermata (product Croptimus) announced a $10M Series A. The author's Brooklyn clinic Fermata shares the name; he expects possible trademark issues between the two companies.
statements.note: Sincere line inside an otherwise satirical post; concerns the author's own company (CONTROL candidate).

statements.quote: As for Fermata, we may have to include Health in the name. Or come up with some other solution.
statements.context: Because of the name clash with the agtech Fermata, the author says his clinic may rename itself 'Fermata Health' or find another solution.
statements.note: Own-company plan; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: Tomorrow, I will write more about health.
statements.context: Essay on the band American Football; the author commits to returning to health topics in the next day's newsletter.
statements.note: Trivial own-newsletter plan; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: Humans have tamed many forces in the natural world; it's easy to imagine we will continue to do so.
statements.context: Meditation on the January 2025 Los Angeles fires. General claim that humans will keep taming natural forces, immediately qualified by 'Los Angeles proves that not all forces are within our control.'
statements.confidence_phrase: it's easy to imagine we will
statements.note: Vague general claim close to a truism; logged for recall.

statements.quote: Big Health companies—which we used to think of as insurance companies prior to this article— are using prior authorization to maximize their profits. I don't think they're gonna give it up without a fight.
statements.context: Prior-authorization essay (UnitedHealth Group paging a surgeon out of the operating room as the example). The author predicts large health insurers will not relinquish prior authorization without a fight.
statements.note: Negative call about payer behavior; undated.

statements.quote: I don't think this would be a very popular job among insurance company doctors. I think it's likely they would run out of physicians willing to get in a plane just to go meet their colleagues and demand an explanation.
statements.context: Conditional on the author's proposal that every prior-authorization request be delivered in person by a licensed payer physician: he predicts insurers would run out of physicians willing to do it, making prior auth 'endlessly painful to request'.
statements.note: Conditional on a hypothetical legal proposal the author is advocating; unlikely to be resolvable.

statements.quote: Tonight, we kick off the JPM Health conference in SF.
statements.context: Promo at the top of the psilocybin-trial walkthrough: the RAMHT SF 2025 event on January 12, 2025 opens JPM Healthcare conference week in San Francisco.
statements.note: Own-event logistics; CONTROL candidate.

statements.quote: Oh my God, a lot of people will want to get into a psilocybin trial!
statements.context: Walkthrough of the JAMA Network Open RCT of psilocybin vs niacin in depressed frontline healthcare workers (Back et al. 2024; 2,247 applied online, 30 randomized, 100% guessed their arm). The author's stated takeaway generalizes that psilocybin trials will attract many would-be participants.
statements.note: General claim about future psilocybin trial recruitment demand, drawn from one trial's CONSORT numbers.
